qt: to the Commission Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Cornelia Ernst (The Left), Udo Bullmann (S&D), Malin Björk (The Left), Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Following the recent article by Lighthouse Reports1 revealing coordination between Frontex and the Maltese authorities with the brutal Tareq-Bin-Zeyad-Brigade militia in Libya, very serious concerns have again been raised regarding the EU’s relationship with, and financing of, actors in Libya. The Tareq-Bin-Zeyad-Brigade, which is under the command of the son of warlord Khalifa Haftar, was found liable for war crimes by the United States and is known for its cooperation with the Wagner Group. As stated in the article, the group has been actively carrying out pullbacks of persons in distress at sea to Libya, where migrants face systematic and grave human rights violations. The article provides evidence – operational reports of the Irini mission – that the Commission and Member States knew about the activities of the militia. However, nothing suggests a change in the EU’s policy regarding the Central Mediterranean route. 1.
On what legal basis can the Commission or Frontex strive to prevent persons from fleeing torture, inhumane or degrading treatment or other forms of human rights violations?
Does the Commission consider the Tareq-Bin-Zeyad-Brigade to be part of the Libyan Coast Guard?
What kind of investigations are ongoing to examine the scope of EU and Member State activities leading to pullbacks by the militia?
at: (English version) to the Commission Erik Marquardt (Verts/ALE), Saskia Bricmont (Verts/ALE), Cornelia Ernst (The Left), Udo Bullmann (S&D), Malin Björk (The Left), Alice Kuhnke (Verts/ALE), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE) (10 January 2024) Subject: EU ‘cooperation’ with militia to enable pullbacks to Libya Following the recent article by Lighthouse Reports (1) revealing coordination between Frontex and the Maltese authorities with the brutal Tareq-Bin-Zeyad-Brigade militia in Libya, very serious concerns have again been raised regarding the EU’s relationship with, and financing of, actors in Libya. The Tareq-Bin-Zeyad-Brigade, which is under the command of the son of warlord Khalifa Haftar, was found liable for war crimes by the United States and is known for its cooperation with the Wagner Group. As stated in the article, the group has been actively carrying out pullbacks of persons in distress at sea to Libya, where migrants face systematic and grave human rights violations. The article provides evidence — operational reports of the Irini mission — that the Commission and Member States knew about the activities of the militia. However, nothing suggests a change in the EU’s policy regarding the Central Mediterranean route. 1. On what legal basis can the Commission or Frontex strive to prevent persons from fleeing torture, inhumane or degrading treatment or other forms of human rights violations? 2.
Does the Commission consider the Tareq-Bin-Zeyad-Brigade to be part of the Libyan Coast Guard?

3. What kind of investigations are ongoing to examine the scope of EU and Member State activities leading to pullbacks by the militia? (14 March 2024) 1. Neither the Commission nor the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) prohibits individuals from ‘fleeing torture, inhumane or degrading treatment or other forms of human rights violations’. 2. The Libyan Coast Guard is organisationally part of the Libyan Navy (which is under the control of the Government of National Unity). The Tariq Bin Zeyad Brigade is not. 3. The competence for conducting search and rescue operations and organising relevant investigations lies with the Member States. In the letter of 15 January 2024 to the Chair of the European Parliament’s Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs (LIBE), the Executive Director of Frontex confirmed that the Agency has never had direct communication with the Tareq Bin Zeyad. The situation reported in the article cited by the Honourable Members may refer to the issuance by Frontex of a Mayday Relay call over open radio frequencies. Such calls are issued when a Frontex asset encounters a situation where it believes lives to be in imminent danger, such as persons on board an unseaworthy vessel in open water. Upon receiving a Mayday Relay, the relevant national authorities assume the responsibility to organise and coordinate search and rescue operations. Mayday Relay calls are issued on open frequencies and can be received by any vessel in the vicinity, which ensures the fastest rescue response possible.
